title: scheduled-model-warmup-cache-amplification-and-autoscaler-oscillation-runbook-draft
content:
Context
---
We observed repeated nightly throughput spikes in dedicated GPU pools coincident with a scheduled model warmup job (cron: daily 02:00 UTC). These spikes produced a cascade of KV cache misses, allocator churn, and transient autoscaler oscillation in affected pools. Impact: latency SLO violations for tenant inference requests for ~12–25 minutes across multiple regions during warmup windows.

Purpose of this doc
---
Working runbook draft for on-call SREs to: (1) quickly detect and mitigate warmup-triggered pool degradation, (2) collect evidence for post-incident action, and (3) provide safe temporary workarounds while engineering implements longer-term controls (rate-limits, priority routing, autoscaler damping).

High-level hypothesis
---
- Warmup job issues many synthetic requests with large context prefixes and low cache reuse.
- This floods per-GPU KV caches and forces eviction/rehydration storms for live tenants.
- The autoscaler measures increased CPU/GPU utilization and enqueues scale-up, followed by rapid scale-down when warmup finishes — causing oscillation and scheduling churn.
- No explicit traffic classification for warmup traffic (it looks like normal user traffic to schedulers/routing), so it competes with production and triggers eviction thresholds.

Signals to check (fast)
---
- Dashboards: dedicated-pool-p99-latency, pool-request-rate, kv-cache-hit-rate, allocator-requeue-rate, pod-start-duration.
- PromQL quick checks: 
  - rate(http_requests_total[5m]) by (pool)
  - avg_over_time(kv_cache_hit_rate[5m]) by (pool)
  - increase(gpu_utilization_seconds_total[5m])
  - increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h]) for scheduler pods
- Logs: filter ingress logs for user-agent or request-path used by warmup (pattern: /warmup/ or user-agent: model-warmup-bot).
- Correlate with cron schedule: check cluster cronjobs and airflow DAG runs around the spike.

On-call immediate mitigation checklist (for first 30 minutes)
---
1) Confirm warmup window correlation
   - Check airflow or CronJob run times (kubectl get cronjob -n infra model-warmup -o yaml)
   - Slack: ping #infra-ops, look for scheduled-run announcements
2) Classify traffic quickly
   - Ingest logs: grep warmup user-agent / query param across last 30m to estimate QPS fraction
3) If warmup QPS > 10% and latency SLOs breached -> take conservative mitigations:
   - Option A (preferred, low blast): Re-route warmup traffic to non-production burst pools
     - If warmup has identifiable header or user-agent, add temporary route in routing config: tag warmup -> burst-pool (carry low-priority flag).
     - Command: POST to routing-admin /routes with condition user_agent contains "model-warmup-bot" -> target burst-pool-id
   - Option B (when routing change not possible quickly): Pause warmup job
     - In Airflow: mark DAG as paused or delay next run by +30 min (only after coordinating with ML owner).
     - In Kubernetes CronJob: kubectl annotate cronjob model-warmup paused=true -n infra && kubectl scale cronjob/model-warmup --replicas=0 (note: scaling CronJob doesn't stop job in-flight; prefer pausing at scheduler layer).
   - Option C (temporary autoscaler damping): Increase autoscaler stabilization window for affected pools to reduce oscillation risk
     - Edit HorizontalPodAutoscaler or custom autoscaler policy to add scale-down stabilization 10m, and scale-up smoothing 60s.
3) Reduce eviction pressure
   - Lower tenant eviction aggressiveness temporarily: up the eviction thresholds by 5–10% via feature-flag or runtime flag. (Coordination required with SRE/Serving runtime owner)
4) Communicate
   - Post to #oncall-status and #infra-ops with summary: what, impact, mitigation, commit to next steps, mention JIRA-OPS-1427.

Diagnostics to collect (for postmortem)
---
- Timeline of metric traces (5-min resolution) for the warmup window: request-rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, kv_cache_hits, allocator_requeues, pod_scheduling_latency.
- Raw ingress samples (anonymized) of warmup requests.
- Cronjob/DAG run logs and timestamps.
- Node-level GPU telemetry (temperature, frequency), to detect thermal or firmware-induced slowdowns.
- Autoscaler decision logs: scale events and reasoning.
- Which tenants were impacted (tenant IDs from request logs) and their SLA tier.

Root cause hypotheses (to be validated)
---
- H1: Warmup traffic pattern creates low-locality KV lookups (prefix lengths large) -> large cache churn.
- H2: Warmup runs against same model version pinned to production pools, causing cache hotspots.
- H3: Autoscaler config uses short smoothing windows tuned for latency sensitive workloads and reacts to warmup spike as sustained load.
- H4: Routing lacks request-level priority flagging; warmup indistinguishable from production traffic.

Short-term engineering tasks (next 1–2 weeks)
---
- Add warmup user-agent and route rule: ensure warmup requests carry a header X-Warmup: true and are routed to burst/backfill pools. Owner: Marco.
- Implement a warmup-side rate limiter (token-bucket) baked into DAG / CronJob wrapper to cap burst QPS per-region. Owner: ML infra.
- Autoscaler config change: adopt asymmetric smoothing (scale-up fast, scale-down slow) for dedicated pools running production+warmup. Owner: SRE.
- Add kv cache telemetry per-tenant and synthetic warmup probe to measure cache amplification. Owner: Serving runtime team.

Long-term (quarter roadmap)
---
- Warmup-aware placement: create a lightweight placement class for warmup traffic that prefers burst-only nodes and doesn't evict production.
- Capacity planning: build synthetic-warmup capacity budget and incorporate into committed capacity planning for Dedicated.
- Experiment: have model warmup use smaller context-size synthetic traces that better mirror steady state, not huge prefixes that cause eviction storms.

Runbook appendix: step-by-step commands (copy-paste)
---
- Check CronJobs/DAG runs
  - kubectl get cronjob -n infra | grep warmup
  - airflow dags list-runs -d model_warmup --state running --start_date "$(date -d '30 minutes ago' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M)"
- Find warmup QPS in logs
  - gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_container" AND labels.k8s-pod/app="ingress" AND jsonPayload.request.user_agent: "model-warmup"' --limit 1000 --format json | jq '.[] | {ts: .timestamp, path: .jsonPayload.request.path}' | wc -l
- Quick PromQL snippets to paste into Prometheus: 
  - sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="ingress",user_agent="model-warmup"}[5m])) by (cluster, pool)
  - avg_over_time(kv_cache_hit_rate{pool=~"dedicated-.*"}[5m])
- Change autoscaler damping (k8s HPA example):
  - kubectl patch hpa dedicated-pool-hpa -n redwood --type merge -p '{"spec":{"behavior":{"scaleDown":{"stabilizationWindowSeconds":600}}}}'

Escalation and ownership
---
- If mitigation fails and >30 minutes of SLO breaches, page oncall-plat-lead and responsible oncall for serving-runtime (names in /oncall/rotation).
- Postmortem owner: eng-sre (Priya Nayar) + serving-runtime (Daniel Kim). Set Sev-2 if production latency for multiple customers exceeds SLO and persists >30m.

Open questions
---
- Do ML owners require full-model warmups (large prefix) to reduce cold-start quality regressions, or can we use smaller targeted traces?
- Is there appetite for adding request-level priority headers across other ML pipelines?

Notes-to-self / TODOs
---
- Follow up with Marco on routing change PR and a quick canary of warmup header enforcement.
- Create a synthetic-warmup test that simulates real world prefix distribution and evaluate cache impact.
- Draft communication for customers if we need scheduled warmup maintenance windows.

Appendix: snippets for postmortem narrative
---
- Summary: Nightly model warmup job generated a high-QPS burst of low-cache-locality requests that overwhelmed KV caches and produced autoscaler oscillation; mitigations were routing warmup to burst pool and increasing autoscaler stabilization window; medium-term fixes planned include warmup tagging, rate-limits, and warmup-aware placement.
- Key metrics to include in postmortem: p99 latency delta, kv cache hit-rate drop, number of scale events, number of impacted tenants, duration of SLO breaches.
